title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 21: God's Commandment of Love
keywords: to love without counting the cost
primary_topics: Chapter 21 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's reflection on the gospel reading John 13:31-35, printed in BLD Counsels on May 19, 1992, arguing that 'Love is the distinguishing mark of a Christian disciple'

The distinction he builds between the synoptic command to love one's neighbor as oneself and John's command that disciples 'love one another' as much as 'my love has been for you' -- the first human, the second divine

His measure of divine love, taken from St. Paul (Phil. 2:5-11): Christ's humility and obedience 'accepting even death, death on a cross,' so that loving like God means offering one's own life rather than merely preserving it

The application to the Bukas Loob sa Diyos community: because BLD members are bound by 'a solemn written covenant to love one another as He loves us,' their praying, tending, worshipping, sacrificing and serving inside the community must exceed the same acts done outside it
sub_topics: He opens with the thesis that love is the mark of discipleship, drawn from 'our Lord's new and most important commandment, "Love one another"'
He notes the audience of that commandment -- the disciples gathered at the cenacle, 'excluding Judas'
He sets the synoptic parallels beside it (Matt. 22, Mark 12, Luke 10), where Jesus, asked by the Pharisees which commandment was 'the greatest,' answered love of God first and love of neighbor second
He grants that both John and the synoptics make love supreme, but insists the degree demanded between disciples is 'far greater' than that owed a 'mere "neighbor"'

He draws the line between addressees: a non-disciple -- 'Pharisee,' 'scribe' or 'lawyer' -- is told to love his neighbor as himself, while disciples are commanded to love one another as Christ loved them
He names the two loves: love of neighbor is human because it equals self-love, love of a fellow disciple is divine because it equals 'God's love for his followers'
He supplies the measure from St. Paul's hymn (Phil. 2:5-11) -- humility and obedience to the Father's will, 'accepting even death, death on a cross'
He contrasts the two standards in practice: loving like a man preserves life, loving like God 'consists in being Christ' and offering that life so fellow disciples may be saved

He translates the command into BLD terms: love for those outside the community is human and quantifiable, love for fellow members should be divine and therefore immeasurable -- 'to love without counting the cost, as St. Francis says'
He grounds the higher duty in the community's bond: BLD disciples are joined 'not just by common faith and worship, but by a solemn written covenant to love one another as He loves us'

He lists the concrete acts -- praying for healing, tending the lambs, worshipping at prayer meetings, sacrificing to contribute to the BYOP, serving in apostolates and ministries -- and demands each be done more intensely inside the community than outside

He closes with the day's other readings: Paul and Barnabas encouraging disciples 'to persevere in the faith,' and the promised reward of God dwelling among His people and wiping 'every tear from (our) eyes'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 21 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the short reflection Artemio V. Panganiban was asked to write on the gospel reading John 13:31-35 for the fifth Sunday of Lent in 1992, printed in BLD Counsels on May 19, 1992. He began with the thesis that 'Love is the distinguishing mark of a Christian disciple,' drawn from 'our Lord's new and most important commandment, "Love one another"' -- noting that it was addressed to the disciples gathered at the cenacle, 'excluding Judas.' He then set the synoptic parallels beside it (Matt. 22, Mark 12, Luke 10), where the Pharisees ask which commandment is 'the greatest' and Jesus answers first 'You shall love the Lord your God' and second 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' Both John and the synoptics make love supreme, he granted, but the degree demanded of one disciple toward another is 'far greater' than that owed a 'mere "neighbor"': a non-disciple -- 'Pharisee,' 'scribe' or 'lawyer' -- is told to love his neighbor as himself, while disciples are commanded to love one another as much as 'my love has been for you.' Hence neighbor-love is human, being equal to a man's love for himself, while love for a fellow disciple is divine, being equivalent to God's love for His followers. For the measure of that divine love he turned to St. Paul (Phil. 2:5-11): Christ's humility and obedience to the Father's will, 'accepting even death, death on a cross.' To love like a man is to preserve life; to love like God 'goes beyond preserving life' and 'consists in being Christ' -- offering one's life so that fellow disciples may be saved. Translating the command into Bukas Loob sa Diyos, he wrote that love for those outside the community is human and quantifiable while love for fellow BLD members should be divine and therefore immeasurable, 'to love without counting the cost, as St. Francis says,' since BLD disciples are bound 'not just by common faith and worship, but by a solemn written covenant to love one another as He loves us.' Accordingly, praying for healing, tending the lambs, worshipping at prayer meetings, sacrificing for the BYOP and serving in apostolates must all be done more intensely inside the community than outside. He closed with the day's other readings -- Paul and Barnabas encouraging the disciples 'to persevere in the faith,' and the promise that God will dwell among His people and 'wipe every tear from (our) eyes' -- concluding that the everlasting kingdom of divine love 'shall begin in us and with us.'
